In 2021, I was working on a production Flask application when I discovered FastAPI. Type annotations on route parameters, automatic validation through Pydantic, OpenAPI documentation that writes itself. It clicked immediately.

Migrating to FastAPI didn't make sense for that project. The codebase existed, the dependencies were in place, and the churn would have been real for an uncertain gain. But the idea of annotating route handlers and letting the framework handle validation was too good to drop.
The question was obvious: can we have this on Flask?

Flask-Jeroboam is a Flask extension that brings the FastAPI developer experience to the framework. It reads type annotations on route functions, validates requests and serializes responses through Pydantic, and generates OpenAPI docs from function signatures.

The first implementation fit in ~100 lines wired into the application. Enough to validate the idea under real conditions. Late 2022, I decided to go all the way: extract it, structure it as a proper extension, write documentation, publish it.

The project stalled after that. On PyPI, but without a community to keep it alive. In February 2026, I picked it up again with a different intent. I wanted to ask a research question: can Claude contribute quality code to a project that already has five years of history, its own patterns, and decisions to respect? I'm still figuring that out.

Inception — ~100 lines inside a production app

First implementation wired directly into an existing Flask project. Not an extension yet — just enough code to bring FastAPI-style type annotations to existing routes and validate that the idea held up in practice.
Decision to pull the code out of the application. Initial commit in July, first PyPI release in August — basic parser, serializer, Blueprint override, and CI in place.
OutboundHandler, InboundHandler, OpenAPI auto-documentation, and a documentation site. The project then went dormant — present on PyPI, but without traction or community to keep it moving.
v0.1.1 — Flask 3.0 and first stable release
Maintenance release for Flask 3.0 compatibility and updated package metadata. First version without a pre-release suffix — officially stable, though the project remained quiet.
Revival — human-AI experiment on a mature project

Picked up again with a research question that mirrors apicurio-serdes. Where apicurio tests whether Claude can write quality code on a greenfield project, jeroboam asks what comes next — can Claude contribute to a project that already has its own identity, conventions, and an existing codebase to respect?

Complete migration from pydantic v1 to v2, structured in eight phases with 100% coverage maintained throughout. Paired with a toolchain overhaul (uv, ruff, hatch-vcs) and a comprehensive documentation restructure following the Diataxis framework.
Bug fixes for alias serialization and body field edge cases. Ruff rule expansion, xenon complexity enforcement, and OpenSSF Scorecard integration complete the supply chain hardening.
